utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'd like to greet everyone on this Tuesday, 19th of September, 2006. I would like to say good afternoon to the Prosecution. We have the entire Prosecution team today. I would like to greet the Defence counsel and the accused and I am talking to Mr. Pusic. He is not unfortunately here today, I wish him well. But his counsel are here in the courtroom. We hope he will get well very soon and that he will be back with us in the near future. With respect to the hearing today, I will give the floor in a few minutes to Ms. Nozica. We'll have 20 minutes for further cross-examination. With respect to the schedule for this week, following the expert witness we'll have one witness whom I will not name because he will have protection measures -- protective measures under Rule 89. The Prosecution will take ten minutes, and then the Defence will have one hour. Then we'll have a further witness. The Prosecution had envisaged initially two hours and half, but from what I hear the Prosecution will only use up 30 minutes and the Defence will have two hours and 30 minutes for cross-examination. As for the next witness after that, the Prosecution has envisaged 150 minutes for direct examination. The Defence will receive 150 minutes too. And with respect to witness number 3, and again I will not name the witness, we have decided to grant Mr. Praljak 25 additional minutes on top of the time granted to the other accused. That is to say that in total Mr. Praljak will have 50 minutes. In other words, in total the Defence will have three hours for witness number 3 on the list of the Prosecutor. As for number 4, and once again I'm not going to name him for reasons of protective measures, the Prosecution has envisaged 10 minutes for direct examination and the Defence will have one hour. Let me specify with respect to this planning that if we do not waste any time and if we all respect these time limits, it's very well possible that the witness who is currently at number 4, that it's possible for us to be able -- the witness on Wednesday, and this will enable us not to sit on Thursday. But of course this will depend on all of you. That's for the schedule for this week. The Chamber's legal officer has told me that for the record we need to give the names of the witnesses, but I do not believe, as far as I'm concerned, that this is necessary, because the Defence has received the schedule of the Prosecution, and we just need to cross-reference numbers 1, 2 and 3 and 4 with the schedule provided by the Prosecution, because otherwise I would have had to move into private session, and this would have lost us further precious minutes. Without further ado, I'm now going to give the floor to Ms. Nozica for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Tomljanovich.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In your report P 09545, we won't look at it now, in points from 50 to 65, you carried out an analysis of the laws pertaining to the army, the decree on the armed forces of the 3rd of -- of the 3rd of July, and a decision on the basic principles of the organisation of defence from September. Do you remember that? I haven't heard your answer.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As during the examination on the 7th of September, 2006, you spoke of the powers of the head of the defence office in relation to the armed forces. May we look at Exhibit P 000586, page 1. And to remind you, that is the decision on the basic organisation of the defence department. On page 1 in Croatian and on page 3 in English the legal basis of this decision is stated. That's page 2 in Croatian because page 1 is just a title page. It's page 3 in English. Page 2 in Croatian, please. It's efficient for the witness to see the page in Croatian. Yes. We can now look at the first page in Croatian, and here on the first page we see the legal basis for this decision. We can look at it together. It says: "Pursuant to Articles 11 and 29 of the decree on the armed forces, I hereby issue a decision." Is this the legal basis for this decision?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says here in the preamble.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I read Article 11 to you, which is the basis for this decision, so we don't have to look at the decree on the armed forces, but I will read it to you and you will agree with me because I believe you discussed it in your report. It states: "In order to carry out the tasks from Article 11, paragraph 2 of this decree, as part of the defence department the Main Staff shall be established." So the second paragraph is important, and it reads as follows: "The organisation of the Main Staff shall be prescribed by the Supreme Command of the armed forces who shall appoint the leading persons in the Main Staff." Is that correct? I didn't show you Article 11 of the decree on armed forces, but I assume you remember it. So is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the wording specifically, but this seems to be my recollection of what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a look at the decree later on and we'll come back to this if need be. May we look now at page 3 of this decision in Croatian. It's page 6 in English. This is the page on which Article 9 begins. A page further in Croatian, please. The next page, Article 9. Yes. Yes, here it is, B. That's page 6 in English, I think, but we can begin while we're waiting. According to -- well, now we've lost it in Croatian. We had it just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We don't have in English either, so there's no discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it's page 6 in English. Yes. Now we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: According to the provisions of Article 9, paragraph 3, the chief of the Main Staff shall be responsible to -- according to Article 9, paragraph 3, is the chief of the Main Staff responsible to the head of the defence department in relation to all administrative tasks and as regards issues relating to the budget and material supplies and to consumption and general organisation of civilian life? Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the last clause there which I think you may have missed is the wartime organisation of the armed forces. So, yes, everything you said plus the last couple of words there, "and the wartime organisation of the armed forces."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Wartime and peacetime organisation. That's what it says here. I think I read it all.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says, in any event.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please, according to Article 9, paragraph 4, "the chief of the Main Staff shall be directly responsible to the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna for all issues relating to the Supreme Command, unit organisation, strategic and operative plans and the use of the armed forces in time of war or peace." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 of the same article, the one beginning "Brigade commanders," the last paragraph, this prescribes the relation between the brigade commanders and the president of the HZ HB, the head of the defence department, and the chief of the Main Staff. Does it follow from this provision that the brigade commanders are subordinate to and responsible to the head of the defence department for all administrative tasks and issues of budget, material, supplies, consumption, and the overall organisation of life and the organisation of armed forces both in peacetime and in wartime? Does that follow from this article?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that follows from the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Yes, it does follow from the third, but here it's specified that brigade commanders are mentioned. As regards command and the use of the armed forces, are the brigade commanders subordinate and responsible to the chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let's now take a look at the document that we didn't see a moment ago. P 00588. This is the decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And while waiting for it to turn up in e-court, I'll just remind you that the powers of the head of the defence department, which stem from the decree on armed forces and refer to mobilisation, read as follows -- if you want to look at it we will, but listen to me. It says: "For the preparation and carrying out of mobilisation of the armed forces the following shall be responsible ..." That's Article 13 of this decree, "... The head of the defence department for the preparation and carrying out of the mobilisation of the armed forces." My question to you is: Are these the powers described in Article 9, paragraph 3, of the decision on the basic organisation that we have just seen, or are these powers relating to the use of the armed forces? We can look at Article 13. We have this decree before us. Article 13. Excuse me. Actually, it's page 13 in Croatian and 00300135 in English. That's Article 38. 13 in English. 13 in English and 003 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 13 in Croatian, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Article 38, page 13 in Croatian. Now you have it in English, so we can take a look at it. "Persons responsible for the preparation and execution of mobilisation of the armed forces shall be," and I'll read just the part referring to the head of the HVO defence department, he's responsible for preparation and execution of mobilisation of the armed forces. And my question was: Are these the competencies provided for in the article -- the paragraph of the decision that we have just seen? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not entirely sure if I did. If what you're asking is, is this the so the of thing that can be seen in the prior article. As far as I know it could be the sorts of powers they're talking about, although this is dealing specifically with mobilisation. But it doesn't seem to be, at least not in my opinion, in direct contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. That's what I wanted to hear from you. That's what I asked you. In the same decree, Article 41, on page 13. Yes, we have them both now. In order to save time, I will ask you the following: In Article 31 of the same --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 41, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- of the same decree, the competencies of the defence department are described relating to supplying the armed forces with materiel. Are these the competencies described in Article 9, paragraph 3, referring to the head of the defence department, or are those competencies relating to the use of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What does "supplying" mean?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, taking care of and providing material, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. So do you say that these are the powers that the head of the defence department has pursuant to the decree, Article 9, paragraph 3, the decree we just read a little while ago? Do you want me to read you --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: -- that again?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's fine. These are the sorts of things that I would understand that the head of the defence department is supposed to be doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In Article 7 of the decision on ranks, we won't look at it but please listen to me, promotion to a higher rank and transfer as well as uniforms fall within the competence of the defence department, and they confer rank on non-commissioned officers. So is this in accordance with the decree that we have just read, or are these competencies relating to the use of the armed forces? So conferring the rank of an active, non-commissioned officer, is this a competency that the head of the defence department has, according to the decree on organisation. Mr. Tomljanovich, you said you are not a lawyer. We are talking about ministerial and procedural competencies of the head of the defence department. I'm only asking you whether these were the competencies he had pursuant to the decision on the basics of the organisation of the defence department.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should also add I'm not a military officer, but these sorts of things would seem to follow from the decision, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you were asked questions about this, you did say that you were not a military expert, but you did leave open the possibility that the head of the defence department was directly superior to the brigades. You didn't actually affirm this, but you left open the possibility, so I'm trying to go through the competencies of the head of the defence department with you. In Article 34 of the decree on armed forces, and this is quite a contentious article so please listen to me first and then we'll take a look at it. Article 34. We need to go back a little bit. It's Article 34. The competencies of the head of the defence department are listed to appoint and relieve of their duty -- please listen to me first. I'm putting my question now. In Article 34 on the decree on armed forces the competencies of the head of the defence department are listed to appoint and relieve of their duty other officers and commanders, junior officers, except for high-ranking officers. Would this be the competence provided for by that decision that we looked at, Article 9, paragraph 3, or are these -- please listen to me first. I will not deny you the possibility of commenting on Article 34, but listen to my question. The powers referring to the appointment and dismissal of officers, are they among the powers provided for in Article 9, paragraph 3, of the decision on the basics of the organisation of the defence department? Are these administrative tasks, please tell me. And if you can't reply, please say you can't. There's no need to dwell on this because it speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's right that this speaks for itself, and the question of whether it's not administrative depends or your definition of what's administrative, but I do think the article speaks for itself as far as the powers are concerned, or -- this Article 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be more precise. You say that Article 34 speaks for itself. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it clearly says at which levels -- who is to appoint officers at which particular levels and whose duty that is. Appoint and relieve.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave I ask for additional time precisely because of this Article 34 of the decree, because I feel that it is linguistically quite erroneously formulated, but logically the interpretation of this Article 34 is completely different.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You were presented on the 7th of September here in the courtroom the powers relating to appointment and relieving officers in higher positions as well as the powers of the head of the defence department. So please take a good look at Article 34, and tell me logically who is appointed or relieved by the head of the defence department. Can we take a look at it together.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Article 34, paragraph 1 says: "Commanders of the armed forces shall be appointed and relieved of duty ..." That's a general provision relating to all commanders. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was my understanding -- and I do agree it's drafted very badly and that's a problem with the drafting. It's my understanding that the president of the HZ HB goes with the sentence before it or what's preceded by the colon. What's with the colon preceding it, that it would be the president of the HZ HB who commands -- or who appoints and dismisses commanders of the armed forces, and it would be the president -- or the head of the Department of Defence who would appoint and relieve brigade commanders and officers at higher ranks. Well, maybe not, actually, now that I look at the final paragraph. Yeah, because if you look at the time paragraph, then -- hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yourself now say maybe no.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will show you evidence supporting my assertion. So please look at the English version. "Other officers and commanders, junior officers and other military personnel shall also be appointed to or relieved of posts," and so on. You say -- in English it says unspecified in the original. Do you see it in English? But that's because if you look at this article logically it follows that the president of the HZ HB appoints commanders of brigades and high-ranking officers, whereas the head of the defence department and commanders appointed by him appoints other officers and commanders, junior officers, and military personnel, commissioned and non-commissioned officers. Would that be a logical interpretation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would also be a logical interpretation, and I will add that it's written very poorly in the original Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Nozica, could you read paragraph 1, 2, 3, yes, paragraph 3 in your own language so that the interpreters can translate, because we saw that the translation in English, as we see it in the document, has a question mark, and I'd like to have a control effected by the interpreters here from the booth. So read out that paragraph slowly and we'll listen carefully to the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must admit that the paragraph is properly translated, but this dilemma in the translation should be linked to the representative of the defence department and the commander that he authorises. So he appoints the other officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, I have a problem because the English translation that we're looking at here is an approximate one because they've placed a question mark and said, "Unspecified in the original." So what I would like to do now is listen to our interpreters and hear how they're going to interpret paragraph 3, which has been written out in B/C/S. So it's not the English text that leaves room for doubt, it is the B/C/S text that is not quite clear. So would you read out the text, and we're going to listen to the interpretation. It will take two or three minutes. But it's interesting -- it's important for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I know it is, and that is why I asked for additional time. I'll start reading from the beginning, Article 34 from the beginning, because only in that way will we be able to understand the portion that you say is not correctly translated. Now, the first sentence reads's follows: "Commanders of the armed forces shall be appointed and relieved of duty," and then there's a colon and a new line, bullet point: "By the president of the HZ HB." Then there's a full stop. Then after that we come to the following: "Commanders of the brigades and high-ranking officers," then once again a colon and a bullet point, "shall be appointed or replaced by the head of the defence department or by commanders," and then it says, "the other officers and commanders. Other officers and commanders, junior officers, military officials and to officers and junior officer positions of military employees in the armed forces." Now, the colons put in the wrong place have created this dilemma, the dilemma that I tried to clear up with Mr. Tomljanovich. However, I can show Mr. Tomljanovich with respect to the authorisation which allegedly, according to him, in court is what the representative of the defence to appoint officers at high-ranking positions which not -- was not the case both de facto and de jure. So can we just clear up this dilemma, and can we take a look for a moment at 500289. It is the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we examine that, we see that the English translation did not correspond to the text in the B/C/S, because the text in the B/C/S states that the commanding officers, and then there's a colon and a bullet point, are appointed by the president of the HZ HB and by the brigade commanders. So there are two possibilities. According to the French translation, it is properly indicated that the commanding officers, that is to say that can be superior officers, brigade commanders, or lower-ranking officers, and the manner in which they it are appointed can come from various authorities. The president, that's quite normal because he's the Supreme Commander of the army, or by the brigade commanders. So that's how we can understand the text. But you can, of course, put forward another opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I will propose my own reading which does not entirely coincide with that of Judge Antonetti I see a first rule which says commanders of the armed forces will be appointed et cetera by the president. Now the question is, what are the commander are of the armed forces? I think there were four regions if I understand correctly, and I think that these commanders are those four of a region. I'm not quite sure whether these are also identical with the brigades. If they are, then it's still more complicated, because the next paragraph says that brigade commanders, as opposed to commanders of the armed forces, whatever, are appointed by the minister of the defence. I think this entire article is a model of completely failed attempts at regulation. It is not possible to make any sense by reading it. If one were to study this, one would have only one possibility: One would have to study every appointment made in the relevant time and find out exactly what happened. This text, in my view, is completely useless. I'm sorry to say so, but I am duty-bound to be honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have an intervention here from the accused. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to be of assistance to clarify Article 34 in the sense in which it was applied. We can understand it in one way or another but this is the truth, that the Supreme Commander appointed and relieved of duty commanders of brigades, he did that, and high-ranking officers. Now, which high-ranking officers I'll explain. The commanders of operative zones, all the assistant commanders of operative zones, the chief of the Main Staffs and all his assistants and heads. Those are the officers appointed by the Supreme Commander. So this goes down to the level of brigade commander and up to the Main Staff, the chief of the Main Staff. That is the interpretation of Article 34 and that's what was done. The representative of the Defence explained everything lower down. The other assistants, junior officers, and so on and forth. I think there was a misunderstanding before. So that is the truth and that is what happened. The Supreme Commander appoints brigade commanders as the lowest officer and -- or, rather, highest officer and goes to the commanding officers, all the assistant officers of the zones, and all the heads in the Main Staff, all the chiefs of the Main Staff. All the rest are of a lower rank and they are appointed by the representative of the defence department, various employees, clerks, and so on. So that is an interpretation of the article and I think that all those people sitting here with me will bear me out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with the Court's permission, I fully agree with the interpretation given by my colleague Counsel Nozica and what my client General Petkovic has said, and there was no dilemma as far as I was concerned when I asked this witness my questions that the appointment of higher ranking officers and they are enumerated in the first part of the article relates to the president of the HZ HB. It is he who appoints -- the Supreme Commander who appoints these high-ranking officers. Now, when we came to examine the article further, we came to the English text which was completely erroneously translated and we had a very similar debate, and I interrupted that debate by making a conclusion. I drew the conclusion which was essential for my cross-examination and that is that the Main Staff in no way took part in the appointment and release of duty of those high-ranking officers. So I think that the interpretation given by my colleague Counsel Nozica is the right one and that we should correct the English text.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to speak slower. THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I agree with General Petkovic Counsel. That was what it was like in practice. That was how it was implemented and I stand by that. Perhaps on certain occasions there might have been certain slight differences or oscillations given the present situation but in 99.99 per cent of the cases, as General Petkovic said, this was how it was implemented and applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you for all those interventions especially General Petkovic for his assistance intervention because he in fact testified about that. I can't say whether it was so or not but I can say that -- all I can say is that I'm debating this point because on the 7th of September, on page 6316, lines 20 to 23, the interpretation was that the representative of the defence department appoints -- the head of the defence department appoints and relieves of duty high-ranking ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask a question, and I formally put it to the witness, although we seem to have a phase in the proceedings where the accused function as experts and witnesses, and for the record, we don't fail to notice this, that this is a bit special, but it is helpful. Now, the defence -- the Minister of Defence nominates all the other officers and I think that is colonel and from colonel down. Who, and this is my question, who proposes these nominations? Because according to my experience, the role of the Minister of Defence is a relatively formal one and practically it is normally in the line of command that -- where it is possible to assess the qualities of officer -- officers that the proposals are made which in the large majority of cases is the decisive point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That I do not know off the top of my head, who made the nominations. Although I will add in addition to all of this that the longer I look at the original Croatian of Article 34 the more I'm convinced you can come up with either interpretation for it and that it's a problem in the wording of the original, not a problem in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to get in on all this fun that we're having, because everyone just pops up apparently and can just state their opinion whether they're under oath or testifying or not. In the last few minutes among other things there's been different usages of the certainly Supreme Commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to give you the floor, Mr. Scott, because we would like to hear the Prosecution's views concerning Article 34 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution's view, Your Honour, is that we will argue -- just as counsel's -- now all we've done for the last 10 or 15 minutes is argue positions. There's been test -- there's been no essential evidence. Counsel have made their arguments. The accused have stood up and made their arguments. The Prosecution when the time comes will make its arguments in our closing brief. It's our submission that our interpretation is that the president interpret -- the president appoints the commanders in chief, the types of persons such as Mr. Praljak and Mr. Petkovic and the operative zone commanders and the defence -- Department of Defence, head of the department of Defence represents -- appoints the brigade commanders and those next highest ranking officers and that's our position. So as long as everyone is stating a position we'll state our position too. I also want to point out, however, that in the last 15 or 20 minutes the term Supreme Commander has been used in a number of different ways by different people in the courtroom that are not consistent. Mr. Petkovic describe it -- used in one way, somebody else used it a different way. It's been used at least three different ways. We don't know what Supreme Commander means, according to the various people that have used it. But I suggested, Your Honour, that we're way past questioning this witness. All we're doing now is popping up like gophers ought of their holes expressing their views and opinions on what this means and I think we can probably finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have heard different interpretations now of that particular article. According to Counsel Nozica, there is confusion. The accused, I assume as experts in the matter, have provided us with their interpretation, and we have heard the Prosecutor as well. Now I have a brief question for you myself. During your research, did you look at the different appointments ever, zone commanders or brigade commanders, and on the basis your research into that that you could give us your opinion of the practical implementation of that article, that provision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't tell you anything very specific. I believe I have seen appointments of zone commanders in the past. That's not something I looked at for this particular report, although I would recommend I believe that is among the documents which are in the possession of the OTP, those appointments and other appointments, and I would just recommend that instead of worrying about what the intent of Article 34 is that we just simply look at the actual pattern of appointments insofar as we know them. But off the top of my head I don't remember who appointed whom in the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to end quickly now because we've already surpassed the 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Had I not been interrupted, I would have concluded with the several examples that each of you are talking about, and they are all Prosecution exhibits, and that's why I am amazed at the Prosecution's stand today. But we'll go through the documents very quickly now, and when a military expert comes in, if necessary, if this subject is put to him then we'll be able to clarify it when a military expert comes in. But may we have 2D 00141 placed on e-court, please. I'd like to say this is Prosecution Exhibit P 00661. It is the appointment of the commanders of the operative zones, the decree on appointment, and that is precisely what Judge Trechsel referred to. So here we have a decision. It says pursuant to Article 34, paragraph 1 of the decree on the armed forces. So that is the president of the HZ HB and his authorisation. The following are appointed to wartime establishment: Commanders of operative zones, and then you can see for Eastern Herzegovina, Northwestern Herzegovina, and so on, and it is signed by Mate Boban at the bottom. So the proper interpretation of Article 34 is borne out by this. It is the authorisation of the president of the HZ HB. We are now going to look at 2D 00143 that's the next document for the record it is Prosecution Exhibit P 03054. Now, while we're still looking at this document we can look at the date and note that it is the 20th of October, 1992, and I purposely selected documents from different time periods so that we can see, as Mr. Tomljanovich says, that model. Here we have it on our screens. That is the -- the date is the 1st of July, 1993. Once again pursuant to Article 34, paragraph 1 of the decree on the armed forces in the HVO Brigade of Citluk the following are appointed, Stojan Musa, commander of the brigade, brigade commander. So Mate Boban president of the HZ HB is appointing a brigade commander. May we have the next document now, please. 2D 00144. And that is also a Prosecution document P 03363. And I purposely just selected Prosecution documents although there are others too. We haven't got time to look through them all. Yes, that's the document. Can we have look at the date. I think we have it in English, please. It is the 10th of July once again. Once again the President Mate Boban is appointing Alojz Djerek on the same basis of the same legal regulations as brigade commander, isn't that right? With the Court's permission I have two more documents to show. I think it would be useful because of the discussion we've had and dilemmas and I have the decision in order where the head of the defence department is appointing someone so we can see what his duties were. The document is 2D 00145 now. That's the next document, and it is Prosecution Exhibit P 04234. The date is the 16th of August. That's right. We have the new document in Croatian but not in English yet but the date is the 16th of August. Can we lower the document a little. Yes, 16th of August once again. Pursuant to the provisions of Article 34, paragraph 1, item 1 of the decree of the armed forces, President Mate Boban appoints to the Rama Brigade Marinko Zelenika as brigade commander. Isn't that right Mr. Tomljanovich, brigade commander here we have his appointment.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now the last document from this series it is 2D 00146. And I'd also like to mention that it is a Prosecution Exhibit P 06164. This is a document dated the 27th of October, 1993, this time. So we have looked at documents spanning a whole year. Once again we have pursuant to the provisions of Article 34, paragraph 1, item 1 of the decree on the armed forces, the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. So here once again we have a change of function, of post, appoints to the Marichacha [phoen] Brigade, Ivana Saskor [phoen], as brigade commander. And the final document, the appointment by the head of the defence department, let's see whether it was in conformity with Article 34 fully. 2D 00142 is the number of the exhibit. 2D 00142 is the number again. It is a Prosecution document P 0698. Here you have it on the screen. And may we have a look at the last page now, please. Or we needn't -- leaf through it if you believe me it is the head of defence department HZ HB, Bruno Stojic, who signed it, and here once again we see pursuant to article 34, para 1, item 2 of the decree on the armed forces. So that is the logical interpretation of Article 34 whereby the head of the defence department and the commanders that he authorises appoint the other officers and commanders, junior officers, military staff, and so on and so forth. So this decision, this order bears that out. And the date is the 3rd of November, 1990 ... [as interpreted]. We see who Mr. Bruno Stojic appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we can now ask the expert witness what he that is say about all that. Counsel Nozica has shown you a number of orders of appointment signed by Mate Boban appointing different high-ranking officers, brigade commanders, et cetera, and the last document, which is 2D 000142, was the appointment once again by Mr. Stojic with respect to different officers, and it -- in a brigade. The different services, operations, security, intelligence, logistics. The different departments. So what do you have to do say to that, Witness? Does that comply with your vision or not? What can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think these documents, first of all, they are as Ms. Nozica said. I can confirm that. I'm sure these aren't the only appointments we're going to see, and if this is the general pattern, this is the general pattern. All I know is what's in the documents, and I'll state again that if this tends to be the general pattern in the appointments, then that's what we should consider it to have been and I would imagine though that these aren't the final appointments that we've seen, but in this instance, yes, it follows a general pattern. In these instances, four or five instances.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now my last question. This general pattern is that the commanders of the operative zones, the commanders of the brigades, which means commanders and officers high-ranking commanders and officers, according to this general pattern were appointed by the president of the HZ HB. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: From these orders, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Okay. And the other officers, junior officers, lower-ranking staff was the head of the defence department that appointed them. Does that emanate from what we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what's going on in this last document you have up on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I thank you for the time accorded me. I have overstepped my time limit considerably but I consider that it was important to clear up that dilemma. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would sincerely like to thank you for allowing Counsel Nozica to conduct the cross-examination and that she wanted to deal with the interpretation of what we were dealing with, not with putting right translations. I think at a correct reading of rules and regulations is the best way of going about it, and I think that the documents that we discussed a moment ago showed what I wanted to show during my cross-examination, and that is that when we come to important issues related to the armed forces that decisions were made without the Main Staff and that the Main Staff was not the only communication link with the armed forces. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. The Judges will appreciate and make note of what you said. We will have other witnesses, military experts, and I'm sure we'll have ample opportunity to about back to that famous article, Article 34, and discuss it further. If there are no questions from the Prosecution, since the Judges do not have any questions of their own, I would like to thank you, sir, for spending a number of days here in court and answering the questions put to you by one and all. It wasn't an easy job, I am sure, for you to do, but you responded to the questions asked of you. So on behalf of the Judges and on behalf of Mr. Prandler who unfortunately is absent today but will be back with us tomorrow, he -- following Rule 15 bis, I would like to thank you for coming, and we wish you to take up your duties again in the OTP so that after having completed your testimony you can continue to contact the OTP, and the usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn to the Defence counsel for the tendering of exhibits. I assume, Counsel Nozica, that you would like to tender into evidence the documents that you showed. Would you?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Not only these documents but during the cross-examination I had about seven documents previously and the documents today. But I'd like to ask you the following. I know that we -- some exhibits have already been tendered by the Prosecutor during the examination-in-chief, so the Defence of Mr. Stojic would like to state, taking those documents in total, with the acceptance of documents related to the Official Gazette, the example -- because this witness could not confirm, was unable to confirm any of the important points pursuant to your ruling on the introduction of evidence, admittance of evidence, and because all the meetings that were held which presented by the expert witness we have on the Prosecution's list as witnesses who attended those meetings, and therefore I would like to ask you if that is possible. I'm speaking in my own name. I don't know whether my other colleagues will join in, that possibly in due course when we have more time we can tender the documents we wish to enter into evidence and to challenge any documents either in written form or orally as you rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore you have comments about the exhibits that the Prosecution wishes to tender but you'll have to do this later because we don't have any time for this today. Mr. Kovacic, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought it might be useful to tender the document which was discussed at length, and many sides participated, and this was a result exclusively of the badly drafted Croatian in the original. That's P 0061 or D 00041. My proposal is that Your Honours ask CLSS to revise the translation of Article 34 of this decree. It's evident that the translators themselves were in a dilemma. You remember their question marks. But as a person whose native tongue is Croatian, and Judge Trechsel also observed this, it's an evident example of erroneously drafted legislation. But it's also an example of bad Croatian grammar, because there is no subject or predicate in the sentence. Therefore, I propose that Your Honours issue an order to CLSS, because it's very difficult for the interpreters to translate such a text from the booth. So maybe we could ask for a written translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the translation is challenged, the rule is that the Chambers will ask CLSS to translate the relevant text. Therefore, I would like to ask the registrar to request a translation of Article 34 of CLSS. I've taken note of the fact that Ms. Nozica is now asking for more time to make comments about a number of documents. With respect to the documents submitted by Mr. Karnavas and by Ms. Pinter, I see that there's a list there. Ms. Pinter. No, sorry. Sorry. I'm talking to Mr. Karnavas's co-counsel. Sorry. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I did submit a list of the exhibits that the defence of Dr. Prlic wishes to tender after the cross-examination of Mr. Tomljanovich. I will read them for the record. 1D 00525, 1D 00898, P 00817, that's the Prosecution -- that's a Prosecution document so we tender it under that number. 1D 00820, 1D 00821, and there follow two documents which the Defence of General Petkovic allowed us to use, 4D 00022, 4D 00023. And the eighth document is 1D 00918. This is the presidential transcript of the 17th of September, 1992, which was submitted to this Chamber under number P 00498. Yesterday, Mr. Karnavas showed this document to Mr. Tomljanovich with translations of certain pages which the OTP did not submit to Your Honours. In line with Your Honours' guidelines, the pages not translated by the OTP have been added by us to this transcript, and we felt that together with all the pages that have already been translated by the OTP we should put them together to make a single document, because this would then be easier for Your Honours to read. I'm only telling you which pages were translated by the Defence team of Dr. Prlic. I will give you the numbers in e-court. These are pages 1D 33007, to 1D 3300190. The next group is 1D 330032 to 1D 330047. And the third group 1D 330060 to 1D 330065. We have another group of pages translated by the OTP but not submitted with Exhibit P 00498. We don't know why. This may have been an omission or an error, but we have included them in the complete translation in e-court, 1D 330048 to 1D 330059. Altogether, this makes some 40 pages which the Defence team of Dr. Prlic translated for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In order to speed things up and to make things even clearer, I would like to ask Ms. Nozica to look at the document prepared by the Defence of Mr. Prlic. We have a list with the documents tendered, and on the other page we have the documents submitted that the Defence challenged by counsel and the reasons why these documents are challenged. I think this way of going about it is much clearer, but I'm going to give you the floor later this week or this week to tell -- for you to tell us about the documents you're challenging. Let's now move on to the next witness. From what I understand, contrary to what I said before relates -- with respect to witnesses 1, 2, 3 and 4, from what I understand we're going to have Witness 2 first, Islamovic from what I understand. Is that the case? I'm asking the Prosecution to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis will be addressing that, Your Honour. Before we do that I just want to make sure that the record is clear in terms of the Prosecution position on some of these exhibit matters because a number of different things have been said and I think the Prosecution should also have a fair amount of time to respond. The -- number one, Your Honour, we believe that the witness -- the exhibits tendered through this witness should be admitted through the -- by the Prosecution -- or through this Prosecution witness, that it is consistent with ICTY practice for the documents that an expert is used in this way, to be submitted and to be admitted. I also note in this regard that to do otherwise -- but to allow the Defence to tender exhibits through this witness would be completely inconsistent, because apparently on the one than the Defence is saying, well, this witness does not have personal knowledge therefore exhibits can't be admitted. But then they turn around and tender their own documents no different from the Prosecution exhibits and say those should be admitted. Your Honour, you can't -- we can't have two different rules, one for the Defence and one for the Prosecution. So these are all exhibits and materials that have been used by this expert in the preparation of his report and in all respect, Your Honour, with respect to the Chamber we think that all the exhibits tendered through Mr. Tomljanovich by the Prosecution should be admitted. Also, Your Honour, we think it's important to raise and I don't want it to continue any longer without this being addressed it may not be resolved this moment but I want to make the Prosecution position clear, and that is, as the registry has raised, when a Prosecution exhibit numbers are used or when Prosecution exhibits are used, which we don't object to, but they have a P number. And we request, Your Honour, that if a Prosecution document is used that it be admitted under the P number. And I'll tell you why that's important, because at some point we have to continually go back through our records and determine what's been admitted and not admitted, and there is no point for us to tender again a document that has been tendered under a different number. So if it's a number -- if the Prosecution has already numbered her exhibit with a P number and the defence wants to use it, which is fine, then we ask that it be admitted and kept with a P number designation so that we know ultimately which of our exhibits have already admitted and we ask the Chamber to consider that and give us further correction on that but again it can't be a situation where the Defence to admit these exhibits but not for the Prosecution, and it'll be clear that the same P number is used so that we don't have to go back later and try to decide which P numbers have been admitted and which ones have not. On an outstanding matter concerning Mr. Tomljanovich, there was a disputed exhibit from -- concerning the Blaskic diary so-called, which is not in fact what it was. This was on exhibit P 01788. It was an excerpt from the Blaskic diary that was used with this witness. First of all, it was not -- it is not the Blaskic diary, as asserted by Defence counsel. This was the minute book, the official minute book of the HVO Central Bosnia operative zone which is authenticated by Blaskic himself in the Blaskic case. Number two, there was issues about this being an excerpt. The entire minute book, the entire minute book is P 01796, which was disclosed to the Defence for the first time on the 11th of February, 2005, and again on the 19th of January, 2006 and was and is on the Prosecution's 65 ter exhibit list. The excerpt itself is P 01788, which was disclosed to the Defence more than two years ago, more than two years ago on the 6th of August, 2004, and again on the 19th of January, 2006, and was and is on the Prosecution's 65 ter exhibit list. It was also asserted in the courtroom that the Prosecution in the Blaskic case had denied the authenticity of this document. That is not the case. I have reviewed the Blaskic record. It is not the case. Blaskic submitted it, authenticated it as the minute book of the Central Bosnia operative zone and both parties used in the Blaskic case as an authentic document. So it was not correct that it was disputed by the Prosecution in that case. Finally, Your Honour, I want to note that in connection with the witness Galbraith, the Prosecution has filed today two 92 bis motions related directly related to this witness. One is the -- tenders the transcript of Paddy Ashdown from the Blaskic case, which gives a -- directly corroborates Ambassador Galbraith's testimony, talks about his conversation with President Tudjman at a dinner London in 1995 in which Tudjman stated his desires to divide Bosnia with Serbia and drew Mr. Ashdown a map of a divided Bosnia and Herzegovina which is attached to his transcript, that we also -- and if we can go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. Ms. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that we have not tendered any documents because we consider that certain documents used by the expert for his analysis are not exhibits meeting the procedure set out in the instructions issued by Your Honours. So they cannot be admitted into evidence. Apart from this, we propose that part of this report, and I'm referring only to the part on which I examined, the part relating to prisoners and camps, from paragraph 258 to 284, not be admitted, because Mr. Tomljanovich said that he did not have most of the documents relating to this area, and in his report he made general assessments from which one could conclude that he analysed all the documents relating to this area. I retain the right to object in writing to every document tendered with Mr. Tomljanovich, through Mr. Tomljanovich, explaining the reasons for our objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very quickly, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very brief, Your Honours, but I must respond to some things said by the Prosecutor. As far as I'm concerned, we can be in open session. Oh, we are in open session. I apologise. As regards P 1796 mentioned by the Prosecutor, our objections were twofold. The Prosecutor has not responded to our second objection to that document, which was that when preparing for the witness this document was submitted to us only two days before the witness's testimony, and it was not listed in the proofing chart submitted to us for this witness, and that is our objection. It was used as a surprise, and we were unable to prepare for it by checking other documents in the archives and databases we have which would enable us to deal with it. I agree that this document, along with the all the other documents disclosed to us on the 19th of January, '06, in the pre-trial brief was disclosed at that time, but let me remind Your Honours that Your Honours asked that the Prosecutor provide the Court with precise overviews as to what document referred to what count in the indictment and what witness. As we received this document only two weeks ago, we could not anticipate which of the 9.000 or 10.000 documents listed there on the 19th of June the Prosecutor planned to use or not to use through this witness, especially as it was not put on the proofing chart which we got some 10 days or a fortnight before the examination of the witness. The methodology to be followed is that the Prosecutor provides us with a proofing chart telling us what document he wishes to use with the witness and what paragraphs in the indictment the witness is testifying to. We can then prepare. In this case, two days prior to the testimony he pulls out this document and puts it on the table. That's why we propose that P 1796 not be admitted, because documents cannot be produced like this at the last moment. I would also like an explanation in order to stick to deadlines. The Prosecutor, as far as I was able to understand, is planning to submit a motion for the adoption of the testimony of witnesses in other cases, Paddy Ashdown in particular, and he mentioned another name, a former US ambassador, but this was in closed session so I won't say the name now. Would the Prosecutor advise us whether he will make this submission in writing so that we can respond, or must we respond to this ad hoc, oral motion? Your Honours, I wanted to intervene before. Now is obviously not the time. I still have certain exhibits where Your Honours told us to add something, but I will wait for a more convenient time. Everything is ready. Thank you. It's an MFI piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, you said that you had filed a 92 bis motion. I suppose it's written motion. It's not just an oral motion. It's -- I suppose it's a written motion, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the two motions have been filed today as I said as the transcript should show, Your Honour, and of course I understand the Defence will seek to make responses to those, no surprise about that. The final response to Mr. Kovacic, the excerpt P 01788 was additionally disclosed to the Defence on the 30th of August, that it would be used with this witness. It is a page -- the page is themself -- it's about a 2, 3 page document I hardly think that Mr. Kovacic can claim any unfair surprise or prejudice that ample time over the past -- since the 30th of August to prepare to use that document and if he wanted to he could have raised it with the witness at any time. So we don't think that's a proper point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic then I'll give the floor to Mr. Kovacic. But first Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I only wish to ask for your clear instructions. We started a discussion about documents to be tendered through Mr. Tomljanovich, and then we went off in another direction. I know the other Defence teams wish to say something about this, so shall we do so now or later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're still talking about Witness Tomljanovich. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hesitate to waste time, but I do have to object. My learned friend says he disclosed a document to us on the 30th of August. I don't have my agenda with me, but he didn't say how many days it was before the witness began testifying. I think it was two or three days. My colleague says four. But the point is not the number of pages. We have tens of thousands of documents in our databases, and every document we receive from the Prosecutor when we are told that a certain document is to be used with a certain witness, these documents take only two to five minutes to read, but we have to search through the databases to put the document in context, to see what other documents can be linked to it, to see what event it refers to, and so on and so forth. So I cannot be provided with a document only a few days before a witness is to testify if Your Honours have ruled that I have to be provided with it 15 days before. If a new circumstance arises during examination, then of course you have to produce a document unexpectedly, but this was not the case here. There was no new circumstance arising. The Prosecutor had this document. He did provide us with it in January, but I didn't know what document he would be using. How could I know that? He only provided us with this document four days before. So instead of preparing ahead, we have to keep backtracking. We have limited resources. We don't have an army at our disposal. So I object in principle. There's no reason for this document to have been disclosed only four days before the testimony. There's no justified reason for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two points with respect to the problem you've raised. It's something that we've discussed before many times. In our previous rulings, we've asked the Prosecution when they produce, they submit a document at the last minute we ask them to explain the late disclosure of the document, and when a new document is disclosed to the Defence at the last minute, the Judges want to know why the document is being disclosed so late. But let me make a second point. You are saying that you are not in a position to -- to work fairly if the documents are disclosed to you at the last minute. You say the trial then is not fair. But I'm a bit surprised here, Counsel, because this case has started many years ago. You have had time to prepare your case and your strategy, all the more so since you had to prepare a brief in reply to the brief of the Prosecution before the trial. Therefore, your strategy, your case, should have been well prepared at that time. Furthermore, whilst the Prosecution is bringing their -- its witnesses, you are preparing your own witnesses. We are working on the case as a whole, all of us here, and when a document is disclosed to you at the last minute, even if you don't know the document, you still know your case. You still know your case and, therefore, you should be able to cross-examine that witness with that document without any problem, otherwise that would prejudice your client if that was the case. As for the Judges, well, we very often discover at the very last minute the documents being disclosed. However, we manage to ask useful questions. And this should be even more so, more true of your because you have clear vision of your case and you know things we do not know. So we take note of your concerns that are very legitimate, but as far as I'm concerned, I want to draw your attention to the fact that you should not have been taken by surprise by the disclosure of one single document. We only have a few minutes left before the break. With respect to the documents submitted through this expert witness, does anybody want to take the floor? Yes. Counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was waiting for my turn to arrive. The Defence of Mr. Valentin Coric wishes to tender three documents. All three are Prosecution documents, but the Prosecutor did not put them to the witness during examination-in-chief. This was done in cross-examination by the Defence of Mr. Valentin Coric. P 04262, P 00592, and P 02533. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Does another counsel want to take the floor? Well, no more speakers. Oh, no. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just in response to a question Your Honour raised a few moments ago. After the break the witness Nijaz Islamovic will testify. Again, he will be a witness whose testimony will be adduced by written statement pursuant to Rule 89(F). We anticipate, however, due to a number exhibits that we show him that we will spend approximately 30 minutes examining the witness with respect to the documents or the exhibits that have been linked to that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's a quarter to 4.00. We will reconvene at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to make a precision with respect to the documents linked to Witness Tomljanovich. If the Defence has any objections, and we have registered some of them because you rose to your feet, you can of course you can formulate them in writing and we'll give you a deadline until the end of the week. So it would be a better idea if you wrote your objections and that would be a better way of going about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Witness, would you please rise. I just want to check first of all whether you can hear what I'm saying in your own language. If that is the case, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do understand you and I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you give me your name, surname and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness. There is a lot of interference in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters have just told me that they weren't able to hear you. So please speak up and give me your name and surname again and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nijaz Islamovic, born on the 10th of October, in Mostar, and my profession is a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you ever testified before an International Tribunal or a national tribunal about events that took place in your country in 1992 or 1993 or is this the first time that you're testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask you to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to hand to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. I'm going to give you a few explanations before you begin your testimony. Your testimony falls within the procedure of Article 89 of the Rules of Procedure of this Tribunal. The Prosecutor is going to ask you something about a statement you gave to the investigators of the OTP. After that, after the Prosecutor's questions, and the Prosecutor will be taking up half an hour, the Defence counsel representing the accused are sitting to your left, and they're going to conduct what we call the cross-examination. Within the frameworks of the cross-examination, they ask you questions, and they shall be doing that for about two and a half hours. If everything goes to plan, you will be completing your testimony today by 7.00, which means we have three hours at our disposal. Without wasting any more time I'll give the floor to Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Actually, my colleague Ms. Gillett will be conducting the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon. Your Honour, as you know the 89(F) procedure is going to be used for this witness's evidence today and following Your Honour's guidelines that were given in private session on the 13th of September, the Prosecution intends to first provide the Court with a short summary of the witness's statement for the benefit of the public so that they are able to understand the nature of this witness's evidence. Following that, I will go through the procedure that the witness confirms the statement and confirms that it is his signature on the statement and the contents therein. I also, as Mr. Mundis mentioned previously, have some nine exhibits to be tendered through this witness, and I will take him through each of those exhibits, perhaps with some context to each of the exhibits and hope not to take up more than 30 minutes of the Court's time in so doing. Your Honour, to begin with the short summary of the statement, which is not evidence. The witness Nijaz Islamovic worked as a doctor in the municipality of Prozor from 1989 until the end of July, 1993, when he was fired from the Prozor health centre along with all other Muslims working there. At the request of the HVO command or HVO police, during 1993, in particular in July and August of that year, Dr. Islamovic examined prisoners in the Prozor secondary school, the MUP station, the UNIS factory, and in the villages of Duge and Lapsunj.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I ask you, do you remember being interviewed by someone from the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: You mean with me?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: It was in 2001, when I worked in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recall following the interview that was held signing a statement that was prepared and read over to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did you give that statement voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness be shown what has become Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit 09701, bearing the ERN number 0207438 to 0207449, both the English and the B/C/S versions. Perhaps if the witness can be given a hard copy of each version as well, because I understand that the B/C/S can only be shown at one time on the screen, and I believe the markings are made on the English version. For the benefit of the Defence, the statement that I've just provided with the witness is the one that was provided to the Defence previously. Dr. Islamovic, have you had the opportunity to read the statement that is now before you prior to coming into court?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And are those your initials on each of the pages of the statement?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And turning to the last page of the statement, is that your signature on the last page?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Does the contents of the statement reflect what you would say to the Court today?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Having re-read this statement in your own language, are there any errors in the statement that you wish to correct before it is tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are a few technical errors. For example, on page 3 it says that the village of Gracac belonged to Jablanica municipality whereas it belonged to Prozor municipality but it is nearer Jablanica municipality. I think it says the reverse.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And apart from that are there any errors either technical, linguistic or otherwise that you wish to correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: In another spot it says that -- actually, my brother's wife looked for me and not what it says. The kinship relations were erroneously written in.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you provide the page number for the benefit of the Court on which that error occurs.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: It is on page 7. It should read my brother's wife.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are there any other corrections that you would like to make of that nature?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, having made those corrections, do you stand by the contents of the statement as being true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Turning now to the document --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more correction. Not from 1989. I haven't worked from 1989 but from 1976. I was a specialist as of 1989, but as of 1976 I worked as a doctor in the health centre of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that clarification. My mistake. Turning now to the exhibits that the Prosecution intend to tender through this witness, could the witness be shown Exhibit number 09695. Sorry, it may be my mistake. 09685. I think I might have said 95. My apologies. Dr. Islamovic, do you recognise the photograph that is before you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is the secondary school centre in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And is that the secondary school to which you refer in your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown Exhibit number 08994.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Once again, Dr. Islamovic, do you recognise this document that is now before you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is a diagram of the interior of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: When you say "centre," what do you mean by centre?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: The secondary school centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And is this sketch, the diagram, is it one that you yourself produced?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you nonetheless able to use this sketch in describing the interior of the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Would it be possible to have this document put on the ELMO? I believe it would be easier for Dr. Islamovic to verify various parts of this diagram what he's speaking about it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, you see now a diagram that has been placed on the piece of equipment next to you. I wonder if it assists you if you could describe the various compartments that are set out on that diagram to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could point to the actual diagram on the equipment to your right and then the Court can see.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is the entrance, and there was a hallway here. That's where there was a guard. This was a classroom. These are steps going up to the storey above. The staircase. I was on the upper floor just once when the camp was formed and when there were very few prisoners in the camp. I looked into this classroom, then went upstairs to see what the upper floor was like. There were classrooms up there, and there was some blankets around the walls and some sort of mattresses, foam mattresses, and there were several people here. Some people went to work, but I saw that up here there were some prominent people from the various villages. They were well-known people in the village, better-off people. And they were prisoners there. They had been detained. They had been brought from their houses. They did not know why. I saw people from Varvara, and Kovacevo Polje, some people from Prozor. But during the previous regime, they might have been some party leaders or something like that, people who perhaps had shops and who were better off and the rest. And talking -- when I talked to them, they said they didn't know why they were there, what was going to happen to them, but they -- but we talked. They were in a fairly good mood. And that's the only time I went upstairs. The other times that I came --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just pause briefly there. Could you remember when that time that you went upstairs was? What month, if you can remember, and what year.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Later on when I came there were more people from other villages. They were brought in, and I would examine them in this room next to the hall. The young people went out to work, and the elderly people -- well, elderly. Between 50 and 60 years old. I knew some of them. They would say they had some heart problems or respiratory problems. I knew some of them, and I provided them with some medicines. I had medicines for high blood pressure and for pains, rheumatic disorders and so on and so forth. The second time I was there was when the first group had returned after 10 days of digging at Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Again, just to -- sorry to interrupt you again, but when was the second time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: It might have been the beginning of June. And I also examined a few people on that occasion, people who had arrived in the meantime, and I examined a few of those who had come back, who had returned from doing their labour. They were rather frightened. Some of them had injuries. One of them showed me his back. He had some injuries on his back. Other man said he felt chest pains after being beaten. And another man who was a distant cousin of mine said that they had confiscated his shoes and that I should tell his family to bring him another pair because he had to go barefoot. So he also showed me the injuries to his back.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: If you can just --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: And asked me to give him some medicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you enter any of the other rooms or the boxes that we see here on the diagram?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you visit the secondary school in July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went in July, I think twice, and examined people, and also -- yes, I examined patients. But the last time I went I wasn't able to say that they were ill. Before that, I would say that so-and-so was sick and he wouldn't have to go out to work. But then I was no longer allowed to do that.
