The doctor from the HVO and the military hospital would -- Rumbovci, his name was Bosko Skoro, and Mario Budimir, they were called in and they were in charge of either releasing somebody in July from a camp or to say that they didn't have to do any work. The prisoners told me that Dr. Skoro came by frequently, almost every day, and that Mario Budimir was sort of the commander and that he had the authority to let people go. But in July to let them go what did that mean, to release them? Many people didn't have any homes or flats by that time and didn't know where to go so even if they were released they didn't nowhere to go. They had nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... once more. And could the witness now be shown Exhibit 3286. Sorry, I'm not seeing it in front of me. Yes. Sorry. Thank you. Taking a look at this document, Dr. Islamovic, you'll see in point number 2 there's the name of Mario Budimir there. Is that the same person to whom you've just referred?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Have you seen this document previously?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you'll see, if you read in point number 1, where it states that the medical service should provide regular visits by a physician to the building where the arrested Muslims are being kept.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know, apart from yourself, if there were other physicians that were visiting this facility?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, apart from the two doctors I mentioned earlier on who came by. And I think this refers to the HVO medical corps or service. I think that refers to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown Exhibit 9686.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, can you identify any of the buildings shown in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The flag there, where the flag is, that's the building that used to be the SUP. It is now the police station. It was the police station during the war. To the right is the centre of town with the cafes. This is a residential building. Before the police building, police station, is the old building where the policemen had their flats. It was built in the 1950s.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you able to identify the building that's a sort of pinkish colour on the left-hand side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's the building where the policemen lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Is the health centre in which you worked --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: We called it the police building.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Is the health centre in which you worked shown on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. It is to the north, 100 to 150 metres away from this building here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: In relation to the police station that you've described, where would it be?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: It's up the road. This road leads to Rama, and this other road leads to the factory and the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were you able to see the police station from the health centre?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. There are three buildings, but you can't see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. The witness has said that there is a road that leads to Rama, to Prozor. Where are we here?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: This care turning here, that's the direction to Rama. The other road leads to the factory or health centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Dr. Islamovic, which town or village are these buildings that we're looking at in?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: It's in Prozor, the northern part of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Turning now to Exhibit 8998. If the witness could be shown this exhibit, please. And once again, Dr. Islamovic, are you able to identify -- [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: That is a sketch which shows the building, the MUP building, and there's a warehouse that belonged to the former Territorial Defence, and the prisoners were put up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did you make this diagram yourself?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you nonetheless able to use it in describing the interior of the MUP station?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I would always go there for documents if I needed any, and my driving licence after the war, now before. There are a few steps to the entrance. On the right-hand side you have the little duty officer, policeman, and then there's a staircase lead together floor above. On the let are the offices where driving licenses and permits would be issued and then there are two little rooms behind the staircase where people were brought in when -- and were detained when they had committed some offence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you visited the MUP building, where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the MUP building twice. The first time I came together with a nurse, and I think she was a Croat, when I was told by the police who told me that there was a prisoner who was injured. That was during the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And where was this person within the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I found her by the staircase in the corridor. I assume that she was in those premises there, but I found her in the hallway. And the nurse had bandages, the bandages with her to bandage the person who had been injured. When I went in there were a lot of soldiers and policemen there, and he was kneeling by the staircase. He looked very poorly. He seemed to be in shock. He was perspiring a lot. He was pale. And I asked him to show me where he was hurt. I saw that he was all bloody around the stomach area when he opened his shirt. I asked him what had happened, he said, "I couldn't take the torture any more, and I took the knife and inflicted the wounds on myself, stabbed myself." The nurse bandaged his wounds, and I said he would have to undergo an operation --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: -- because it was a serious wound, and then they took him off to Rama, to the hospital there. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: On the second occasion, if you could just say whereabouts in the MUP station you went, to which room or corridor.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: On the second occasion I went to these two rooms, the corridor and these two rooms which were referred to as cells. These were rooms where prisoners were kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown Exhibit 9687.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you able to identify this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is the UNIS factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could the witness now be shown Exhibit 9688.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And again, Dr. Islamovic, are you able to identify any buildings in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you do so, please.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is the secondary school centre, the building with a lot of windows. That's the Vitezit factory, and where the chimney is that's the UNIS factory. That's to the north of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And finally, Dr. Islamovic, you say in your statement that you visited Duge and Lapsunj. How did you come to visit these two villages?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: When I went to Lapsunj I wasn't working any more. I was near Prozor in a village called Borovnica where my wife came from, and one day Nikola Curic, a former school friend of mine from secondary school, arrived, and a man named Ibro Mujanovic, who was a driver, and they asked that on the next day I go with them, first to Lapsunj and then to Duge with a lady doctor --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Dr. Islamovic, but just to ask you do you know what function Nikola Curic had at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was doing something in the civilian protection. He was doing something for civilians. And that's why he -- well, he told me that the commander had changed and that there was a request that we visit those inhabitants of Lapsunj and Duge. He came to fetch me and this lady doctor was there as well, and we went to Lapsunj and then to Duge.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... commander.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: The new commander's name I think was Pavlovic, the new commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Anto [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you recall the name of the old commander, the previous commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. Commander of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Commander of the HVO, Rama, Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown finally Exhibit 4193.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You will see that there is a signature at the bottom of this document. Is this the person to whom you are referring, Dr. Islamovic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And have you seen this order before?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further exhibits to put to Dr. Islamovic, and I would ask to now tender Dr. Islamovic's statement, Exhibit number 09701, together with the exhibits that I have shown to him, Exhibits 03286, 04193, 08994, 08998, 09685, 09686, 09687, and 09688. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Defence for the cross-examination, I have a few short questions to put to the witness. I think these questions are very important. Doctor, when answering some of the questions put to you by the Prosecution, you stated that you met a number of people who were detained, and you mentioned the presence of a soldier on the first floor. Can you confirm that the prisoners that you saw were guarded by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The guard was not upstairs but is he entranceway, in front of the staircase leading upstairs. There was always a guard there. There were drinks there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The guard you saw, did he wear a uniform, insignia? According to you, which unit did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, yes. He had weapons and a uniform. He was probably an HVO soldier. What else could he be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And in the town where you were practising as a doctor, what unit of the HVO was stationed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the HVO Rama Brigade. That's what it was called. Rama, Prozor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Who was the commander of the Rama Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander, well, they chained. We have seen that there was Ante Pavlovic. Before that there was a certain Franjic. And there were others before them, but I can't remember who else there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. These were the questions I wanted to put to the witness. I'm now going to give the floor to the Defence. I'm sure you've come to an agreement on how to divide the time. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, good afternoon. My name is Vesna Alaburic I'm an attorney from Zagreb and in these proceedings I appear for Milivoj Petkovic. In connection with your statement and the exhibits shown to you today I will put a few questions for you, and I believe we will conclude this part of your cross-examination very quickly. Could the witness be shown part of the statement on page 10 of the text in Croatian, the passage before the last. In English it's also on page 10 but the first paragraph. It's at the top of the page. Dr. Islamovic, can you please read the paragraph I wish to refer to. It begins with the words "On the 28th of August, 1993."

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you read this out? I see that we still don't have the document in e-court, but while you are reading I believe that it will appear on the screen. So please begin.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: "On the 28th of August, 1993, when all the people from Prozor were expelled, Dr. Budimir Mario had to give his medical opinion about six prisoners. These prisoners were supposed to be released. The other prisoners from the high school saw that the six were put in a jeep and driven away. They were never seen again."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to read a little more slowly. It will be easier for the interpreters. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: "I was told that amongst them were Alibegovic Avdo. He was my neighbour and around 60 years old and had cancer. Ahmet Hodzic. He was about 47 years old. He had psychological problems. Ibro Purgic, who was also about 47 years. He had a heart attack before the war. Numo Imamovic who was about 50 or 55 years old and suffered from spine problems, and Hasko Hrnic who was about 42 years old and suffered from tuberculosis. These people had been really sick. I had treated them during my three visits in the high school and they had been my patients before the war."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: With reference to these six patients you said they were put in a jeep, driven off, and nobody ever saw them again. Could we please have on e-court Prosecution Exhibit P 04693. P 04693. We also have the Croatian text, so please take a look at this order. We also have it in English. Can you tell us, Dr. Islamovic --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: -- what kind of order is this? Who issued it and when? And does it refer to six patients, those six patients that you mentioned in your statement?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So this is an order issued by commander Anto Pavlovic whom we have already mentioned. It was issued on the 31st of August, 1993, and based on medical examinations in the collection centres, he ordered that these six patients be released and allowed to go home, and the military police was tasked with driving them to Konjic. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That is small difference in the names that you mentioned and the names listed in this order. Would you please tell us whether the difference is because you abbreviated the names?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. He was my next door neighbour, Avdo Alibegovic. His name was actually Abdulah but everybody caught him Avdo. His house was 30 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I wanted you to confirm those were these six patients in spite of the differences in the names.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, all of them. I know them all very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We who come from Bosnia know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are overlapping now, speaking while the previous speaker's translation is still going on. So please keep a break between.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, and to all in the courtroom, especially the interpreters. For a moment I had forgotten that it was not just B/C/S speakers who were in this courtroom. I'll try not to forget this again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, thank you for this clarification. Along with the document put to you by the Prosecutor today, P 04193, could we put it back on e-court again, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment. You've asked a question, but you're already moving on to a new one. Sir, you -- a document was shown to you, and according to that document the six persons who disappeared were supposed to be taken to Konjic. These people, have they disappeared? No one has seen them since?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, nobody ever saw them again. They were supposed to go with a group of people when all the civilian population were expelled on the 28th of August, a village was left behind. It was called Kuloglici. There were some 30 or 50 people there who stayed behind, and three or four days later they were supposed to go towards Konjic like the rest of the population which had left, and then these six, these six prisoners, who were also patients, pursuant to this medical finding they were escorted off and they would be escorted by the police and they would go together with this group of local villagers, but as far as I know all trace of them was lost at that point and nobody ever saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, could we look again at this document that you said something about today. This is Prosecution -- a Prosecution document. It's an order issued by commander Anto Pavlovic that all detained persons under the age of 15 and over the age of 60 as well as all those who are seriously ill should be released. Would you please look at the introductory part, the preamble of this order. I do apologise, but we don't have the document I'm referring to in e-court. It's P 04193. It should be another order issued by Anto Pavlovic. No, it's not this document. P 04193. It's a document we have already seen today on the screens. Ah, here it is. Yes. Now we have the right document. Dr. Islamovic, in the introductory part it says: "Pursuant to the on conclusions of the Rama HVO, meeting number such-and-such, I hereby order," and then it's signed by the commander, Anto Pavlovic, who is the commander of the Rama Brigade. So again this is the HVO. Could you please clarify what kind of HVO Rama meeting is mentioned here where a decision was issued pursuant to which this order was issued?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know that. How could I know that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the Rama HVO?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us what it was, then.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: HVO Rama, well, it's short for Croatian Defence Council Rama. All power, legislative, executive, it was all HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the HVO Rama were the municipal authorities in Rama corresponding to the municipal authorities in the previous system?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that these were civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to say to that. I don't know if there were any civilian authorities at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we please put a document to the witness. It's a document which the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please wait a second. Sorry, Counsel. With respect to this particular question put to the witness, I'd like to ask the following: Witness, Ms. Alaburic has mentioned six people earlier on. You've stated that you knew some of these persons. They've disappeared. After the war, did the civilian authorities produce a document, a certificate, any kind of document related to these people stating that these persons were deceased? Did these persons, did these people appear on that list? Or if that isn't the case, is there anything new about these persons, any news about them being maybe in another country? And to conclude, what is your personal opinion? What do you think about this -- these people who have disappeared if nothing has been heard of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think -- well, these people are listed as missing. There are some 15 or 20.000 people still missing, and I think that these six are among these missing persons, but all these years later they would have turned up. So they went missing in the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier on in answer to Ms. Alaburic about the municipal authorities, you said that there were no municipal authorities at the time. Does that mean that in that town, in that settlement, there was no elected official, administrative official? There was no one who was in a position to take administrative decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't understand these matters very well. I was never -- I never delved in politics. Of course the authorities were elected. It was HVO authority. Now, how far these authorities protected the Bosniak inhabitants in Prozor and in the camps I really don't know. It's a difficult question to answer, because all the inhabitants went through some terrible times. The civilian population did. And the authorities didn't protect them much or help them much. And even when physicians went to visit these two or three villages, well, it was five villages coming into one village. Coming into a house you would have 20, 30 people there, no water, no proper hygienic conditions. When we went to Lapsunj there was no water and it was summertime. There were children there, adults there. It was a catastrophe. Terribly difficult situation for the inhabitants. So they didn't pay much attention to anything like that. They didn't care for civilians much. They didn't pay attention to them. So as far as civilian authorities were concerned, they didn't amount to much. It's difficult to imagine what it looked like and the kind of conditions the people lived in and what their mental state of health was and physical health, because when we visited them the young people would spend their nights hiding in brooks, in gardens. The elderly were left without any medication. They had been expelled from their houses, moved about from place to place. So as far as the civilian authorities were concerned, well, what more can I say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel showed you a document, and when you looked at that document it was 4093 -- 4193, where it said that the HVO of Rama had a meeting on the 11th of August, and the decision was taken to set all persons under the age of 15 or over the age of 63, as well as the sick, anybody who was sick. And Ante Pavlovic, on the 14th of August, compiled an order ordering the liberation of all those persons, that they be set free. Now, what do you think about that? What can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that there weren't any youngsters under the age of 15 or there was nobody over the age of 65 either, 60, 65. And as far as releasing them, the people didn't have anywhere to go. They were left homeless. So many people didn't even want to leave the camp because they didn't know where to go. If they left, if they went to places inhabited by Muslims, some groups would turn up during the night and there was the possibility of them being taken prisoner again and sent to some even worse places and camps. So it was vicious circle.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, from what you've just told us about the fact that Mr. Muslims didn't have anywhere to go, in fact, and they didn't wish to leave the detention centres, would it be right for me to conclude that there were Muslims who voluntarily stayed on in the detention centres then?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who would like to stay on of their own accord in a camp voluntarily, but people just didn't have anywhere to go. They had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but can we clarify some points with respect to civilian authority. Now, from your answer to His Honour, I understood it that you recognise that civilian authority did exist but as far as the Muslim population was concerned it didn't perform its duties as it should have done. Now, I'd like to know whether the civilian authorities did it exist or not? Did any civilian authority exist or not?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, don't ask me about authority. I was never in politics. I never liked power and authority or the authorities, and I never did anything else except my own job. So I don't really understand these matters, the civilian authorities and such. I think there was HVO, authority. Yes, the HVO authorities did exist, and they paid attention to things but not sufficiently. They didn't do enough, especially not for the Muslim population. It was uni-national or one-sided.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, from your answer, I can conclude that you do recognise that civilian authority did exist regardless of what kind of civilian authority it was, good or bad. What I'm interested in now is that we can agree that civilian authorities did exist?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if the HVO had these meetings and made decisions, then it means that it did exist. The authorities did exist, except that it was wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, Dr. Islamovic, does the name Mijo Jozic ring a well?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Mijo Jozic was our municipal president.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Municipal president?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we show P 00382 now, please. It's a Prosecution exhibit. P 00382 is the number. And it is a decision by Mate Boban on the appointment of a municipal HVO of Prozor where it says that Mijo Jozic, the HVO president -- is the HVO president. Can you explain the difference between Prozor and Rama?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's still called Prozor, Rama. Prozor, Rama, whatever. Now, the people on this list, I know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are these all individuals who represent executive power and authority, municipal authority in Prozor or in Rama?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they're all individuals who before the war were in politics as well. Mile Tomic, Nikola Ivic, Marko Dragic, Ivan Miletic, Marko Loncar. They were all people who were high-ranking officials in the system as it existed. They were all in politics, and these are all individuals -- well, that's -- those are the people they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When was this enacted, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. We agree. Now, I'd like to go back to an order now on the release of prisoners under the age of 15 and over the age of 60. If you recall. If not, we can have it back on e-court. Do you remember the document? It was an order issued by a military commander pursuant to an HVO Rama meeting decision. And I'd like you to tell me now whether it would be right to conclude that that military commander passed this order in conformity with a decision made by the civilian authorities of the Prozor or Rama municipalities?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move on. You told us today that Mr. Nikola Curic, who came to fetch you after the Rama Brigade commander was replaced, to help the Muslim population put up in the villages of Lapsunj and Duge, and you told me that he worked for the civilian protection authorities. Tell me now -- or, rather, in your statement, on page 10 you wrote that he wore a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: With an HVO insignia on it.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, everybody had that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I'm interested in. Did everybody at that time wear camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had a pistol as well, as a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Judging by the fact that somebody wore a camouflage uniform, were you able to conclude or did you conclude that that person was a member of some military unit of the Croatian Defence Council, or could that person have been in the civilian defence, for example?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, based on the fact that somebody was wearing camouflage uniform, would you be able to conclude whether that person was on duty at that time, or perhaps the person had been allowed to go home since the army worked in shifts. Do you know this term a "shift army" and what it means when an army is organised by shifts? That is to say you spend two weeks on the battle feed and two weeks away.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that Nikola Curic worked the first shift as we said, during the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: He worked normal working hours, did he?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think he worked during the day normal work, hours and then went home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, we conclude that camouflage -- the fact that somebody was wearing a camouflage uniform did not necessarily mean he was an HVO soldier. Now I'd like to ask you and I don't know how much I am I have at my disposal -- may I take 10 more minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. If you have divided up the time amongst yourselves, amongst the Defence counsel, then there's no problem. If you haven't divided up your time, then the two and a half hours divided by six means 120 minutes plus 30 minutes; 150 minutes divided by six is 25 minutes per counsel, and the registrar is going to tell me exactly, and he says that you have already used 20 minutes, which means theoretically you have five minutes left. Unless the other Defence counsel accord you their time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my time as well. At least a part of my time. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank my colleagues, and then I shall proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, you told us that you left Prozor and moved to your mother-in-law in the village of Borovnica, and in the statement as reason for doing that you state that you did so for your own safety and security, because you were afraid that they would arrest you. I can see you laughing, so I assume you know what I'm going to ask you. Well, go ahead and answer.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in the health centre up until the 27th of July, and on that day when the doctor from Rama came, he told the porter or, rather, the man to tell us that we had all been dismissed, and I was expelled from my flat that same day in the evening, at around 8.00. And I was surprised how they had learnt that I wasn't working any more and I was the only one left in the apartment building. And then with my wife and children I crossed across the hallway and went to stay with a Croatian neighbour of ours, and there was a male nurse with us. We spent the night there because we had -- were told to leave our flat within the space of 15 minutes. My wife paid a neighbour to take us to Borovnica, to my mother-in-law. It's about two kilometres away from Prozor. So that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, what I'm interested in now is this: You left Prozor because you were afraid for your safety.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had no flat. I had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's clear that point up. In your statement, you say that you hid at your mother-in-law's because you were afraid that the HVO would arrest you.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, what I'm interested in knowing is this: Nonetheless, in the middle of the August, 1993, you visited the secondary school centre for the third time at the request of somebody from the HVO, and then when you were requested by people from the HVO, you visited the incarcerated Muslims in the surrounding villages, and on this it is logical to conclude that people in the HVO knew where they were and that they were able to reach you and that they could have arrested you had they wished to do so. So could you explain all this to us?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't hiding from the HVO and from people from Prozor who knew me. I hid at night from groups who would come into the village. I wasn't hiding there the HVO. On the contrary. People knew me. They knew me. I had been working for 15 years before the war. But I hid during the night because you would get groups coming in asking for money, taking people off. So I spent 10 days there. The situation at the time was very bad, because a lot of refugees had come in from Bugojno, and there were conflicts in Bugojno, and the result of that was that a lot of civilians and military personnel, too, came in from Bugojno. And then in Prozor there was general chaos. And I think that in the fire brigade and other places where there were Muslims and several houses in town and people who stayed in their houses had a very hard time of it, because every night was very difficult. That's why I hid. I wasn't hiding from the people who knew him, Nikola Curic, Miletic, and all the others. I was hiding like everybody else who happened to find themselves there, because it was summertime so you could go and take refuge in the forests until 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning and then you would come back. So that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, we who know more about the events in the former Yugoslavia know exactly what you mean when you mention Bugojno and when you say that it was the summer of 1993 and all the rest of it, but I'd like to ask you if possible to explain to Their Honours and everybody else what it was that happened in Bugojno and how many people from Bugojno, how many Croats from Bugojno arrived in the Prozor and Rama area, and in what -- what effect this had in relationships towards the Muslims, and then I'll ask you other questions after that.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I wasn't in town any more, so I can only assume on the basis of what people said who had gone into town that several thousand inhabitants had come in. You could see them. We were up on a hill, and you could see a column of cars moving in a column of five kilometres. You could see the road. You could see the cars. You could see the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, those Croats who were coming in from Bugojno, were they angry for having been expelled from their homes just as the Muslims were when they had been expelled from their homes?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I've sat here patiently listening to this last series of questions, and I fail to see how they are within the scope of the witness's statement, how asking questions about people from Bugojno falls with anything the witness has said today and anything that is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What has Bugojno to do --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain. The topic of Bugojno is not one that I broached but the witness mentioned Bugojno first, and he also mentioned why he was in hiding, and then he explained to us that he wasn't hiding from the HVO but that he was in fact hiding from the groups of men who had escaped HVO control and who went round looting people and jeopardising their safety and security. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He broached an essential point and then immediately you moved on to the question of Bugojno. But let's go back to what he was saying, because that's what the Judges are interested in, because we have to rule on the question. You said a moment ago that you went into hiding. You did not hide from the HVO people, because you knew them. You were a doctor and so on. But you said that during the night there were groups who came in, who stormed apartments and houses, and some people asked for ransom or money or whatever. Could you explain what you were saying? Who were these people in those groups? Were they Muslims? Were they Croats? Were they HVO men? Who were these groups? Who made up these groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in Prozor there was a well-known group called the Kinder Platoon, kinder vod. They were young people, ranging in age between 16 to 20, the kinder platoon, 20 or 30 of them, and these young men, some Muslims complained at the beginning and Mijo Jozic said for example that they were out of control and that they couldn't do anything with them or about them. They were young men who were from the villages who took over the Muslim flats, cars, drink, whatever, and then during the night -- I can't call them hooligans but they were bandits. I think bandit is stronger word than hooligan. Anyway they were young guys who would storm the area during the night and did the worst kind of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But these young people, were they armed? Did they wear a uniform? Did they have a chief of some kind, somebody in charge? Could you tell us more about those young people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, those young men were armed, and they had a house where they spent their time mostly, and each of them had a flat, of course. But at night they would come in and their surnames were well known and their cars were well known. If they had a white Lada car or what was called Papak or if their name was Papak, there was Beljo, Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you can give us the names of those people, can you? Can you give us their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zoran Papak was one of them, I think. Then there was Pavkovic. His first name was Tome or Vlado. Then there was Beljo. I don't know. I know them by their surnames mostly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were they Croats, Muslims? What ethnic group did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were Croats from Prozor and from the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So they were Croats from Prozor. Now, you said that President Jozic Jovic [as interpreted] was informed about that, knew about that. And he couldn't do anything about it? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think he could, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this Rama Brigade, did nobody go and see Mr. Ante Pavlovic to deal with the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know who could approach him, because they were all in the camps and helpless there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just explained to us that there was a group of young men, a band of young men who sowed terror amongst the population. But apparently there was also an HVO unit also bearing arms and that the head of the HVO who issued an order, and we read that order, could be the legal authority in a capacity to solve the problem. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if the will was there then a way might have been found, but maybe they didn't dare come into conflict with them either. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, are you saying that these gangs only attacked Muslims, or did they equally attack Croat persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that they attacked Croats. They may have done. They may have taken something from someone at night, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One night while I was at Borovnica hiding in the cellar, one of these groups arrived in the house where my wife was and some other people, and this Papak, it was 2.00 at night. He was taken off for an interview, and the children were screaming, and then he brought him back. So I have first-hand experience of all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. This has not been very clear. At 2.00 in the night Papak turned up at the house where you were hiding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the basement, a small basement downstairs, and they came to the area where we lived, of course. My brother-in-law and I were hiding under the ground, and we heard a car arrive and stop, and then we heard a commotion upstairs. And when they had left, this lady said that they wanted to take her away, but the other guy who was there said, "Look, there are small children here. Leave her," and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This corrects the transcript where it was said "He was taken for an interview," and that one could think that this was Papak, but that is an error obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, one last question about this matter. You stated that you were not afraid of the HVO because you knew many members of the HVO, and you said that the HVO was in charge of the administration of your village at that time. But you also stated that it's something you don't know much about, civilian authorities or military authorities, but you stated that the HVO was in charge of the administration. You knew the people in charge at the time, the authorities, and you were witness of what these young people were doing at night. Did you ever go to the HVO people to ask them what was going on and, then, if so, what was their reaction? Because we have to determine what are the responsibilities, who was responsible for these situations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as the situation developed in Prozor, when I was already in Borovnica and later at Vogoca, I really couldn't move around, and as tensions escalated and conflicts and the situation deteriorated day by day, my wife went to see my colleagues on several occasions to ask them to help us go to Split, and they wouldn't help me. So how could we ask them to do more, to calm down a gang? If a colleague wouldn't help me, then why would the got or the authorities want to help me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A personal question, sir. Is your wife also a Muslim, a Bosniak, or is she of some other ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Let me say once again. When we're at Podgradje where I was born, from September to December, these groups would arrive there was a man called Vukoja who would come with a lad from Croatia to take my sister-in-law and my wife and the children and he took 3.000 marks them and a bag and then he left. So they were robbed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that your family was victim of some racketeering or extortion because they stole 3.000 marks from you, and you're saying that the Vukoza [phoen] was a member of that group, but when they arrived these people, were they -- how were they dressed? Did they wear uniforms, civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: They were all wearing military uniforms. Nobody walked around in civilian clothes. I mean, among the Croats. They were all in uniform, and they were all armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There is now a contrast between what is stated in your statement, and it is the last paragraph of page 10 in the English text, and what is in the courtroom now. What you have said is your wife had the intention to leave and paid 3.000 Deutschmark to be safely led to -- I think to Croatia, across the border. Is that the real story? And then -- and then those people had taken the money, but instead of furnishing the service that they pretended to sell, they simply absconded, so that in fact you were cheated rather than robbed or embezzled.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was this lad with a Croatian uniform, and he was very polite, and my wife believed him. Later, Vukoja turned up with him when they came by car, and then they lost their money and were left on their threshold. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If Ms. Alaburic will allow me just before she resumes, there was an objection made by the Prosecution that Ms. Alaburic's cross-examination was outside the scope of the statement. Your Honour, that's not an objection. There was -- it is true in the case of one witness, Mr. Galbraith, an order was made in his particular case that cross-examination should be limited to the scope of direct examination, but in normal circumstances Rule 90(H) is quite clear that cross-examiner may also go into matters relevant to the case of the cross-examining party even though those matters may not have been dealt with. Your Honour, that's not a proper objection, and Ms. Alaburic's cross-examination, in my submission, was entirely proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not a question of whether the matters have been dealt with or not by the Prosecution. It's a question of the relevance of this witness's evidence, what is in his statement and as it is before the Court. It is not that I have adduced evidence from this witness. The statement is very clear in what it says and the scope of the statement has been also made clear both in terms of the charts that were submitted and the paragraphs to which this statement pertains, and indeed by reading the statement itself. I don't see what relevance that line of questioning has to this witness's evidence, and that's the objection, not whether the Prosecution have dealt with this or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a matter whether the Defence considers that it is relevant to an issue that the Defence wishes to raise and that's not a matter which Ms. Gillett is capable really of dealing with. It's a matter for the discretion of the cross-examiner as long as it appears to the Court to be basically relevant, and that's what Ms. Alaburic was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the Judges, all questions are relevant if they relate to the indictment, to the testimony of the witness, to the answers provided to the questions. So up until now, I do not see in what way the Defence would have not followed these principles. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. By your leave, let us clarify what happened in Prozor and Rama after the arrival of the Croats from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And I wish to clarify another issue raised in your answer to Judge Antonetti's question, His Honour's question, and that's the possibility that military units of the HVO on the territories of Prozor and Rama could have prevented the activity of the hooligan groups who were causing great harm to the Muslim population. Although you did not engage in politics, Dr. Islamovic, based on the general knowledge of all of us living on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, you will be able to answer the following question: Was the army authorised to issue decisions on dealing with gangs of hooligans, or did the decision on this rest with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the decision was supposed to be issued by the civilian authorities. The army could carry out such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the MUP building. Can you tell us whether at that time on the territory of Prozor or Rama there was a police force? Were there bodies in existence which were supposed to ensure security and safety in the town and in other places? If you don't know, then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I really don't know. I think that the policemen whom I knew from before the war and who stayed in the police continued doing their job, but what their powers were and whether they were able to oppose someone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to take the break, but still, that question is of great interest. At the time when you were in Prozor yourself and these gangs were doing what they were doing, at the time were there members of the MUP in Prozor? Were there members of the MUP or had they disappeared? Was there no one left from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't go around in the evenings, by night, so I don't know whether there were any police patrols, whether they were actually doing their job. Evidently they weren't doing it very well, because nobody visited these places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but assuming that no one went outside because everyone was scared. That's perfectly understandable. But in the morning when these gangs had left, in the morning, what did prevent you or other people to go to the MUP building to report what had happened, to lodge a complaint? Was this possible or was this totally impossible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it was feasible. When these groups first appeared, I know that a group of women went to see Jozic, the president of the municipality. They asked that something be done. They even said, "Give us buses," as Jasurevic gave the Muslims buses in Trebinje. That was seen on television. So they could leave, because the maltreatment by night had become very frequent. A group of women went to Jozic, but it didn't help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a quarter to 6.00. We have, unfortunately, to take a break. We will resume at five past 6.00, in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. But there is a point I wanted to check with you, Witness. In your written statement, you talk about what happened during the night in the month of August, and you mention Papak, the famous Papak. But you also stated that three HVO soldiers came, and earlier on you said there were young people, hooligans, and so on and so forth. But these people who came, were they soldiers of the HVO, because that's what you seem to be saying in your written statement, or were these people young people who -- from whom you do not know if at night they were -- during the day they were HVO soldiers and at night hooligans? Can you please specify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think they were members of the HVO. That was the unit called the kinder platoon, 20 or 30 young men. I don't think they were in the HVO, but they were armed and they wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the registrar to display page 7 of the written statement of the witness in English. Page 7 in English. Page 0207441. Very well. If you look at the third paragraph, you will see that you state that one night in August, at 2.00, whilst your family and yourself were in the house, three HVO soldiers came in the house. Then you tell about what happened. Here it says three in English. Three soldiers of the HVO came in the house. And then at the next paragraph you state that one of them was called Papak Zoran. So that's what I'm trying to clarify, you see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. One of them was called Zoran Papak. He drove a white Lada. He was bald, his head was shaved, and he wore an earring. So he was very recognisable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. He wore an earring. But I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that at the beginning you stated that three HVO soldiers came to your house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what happened? Did the investigator misunderstand you? Was there some sort of confusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all those who wore uniforms, that was the HVO. Maybe I didn't -- well, it was an HVO uniform. We considered them to be HVO soldiers. They all wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So would you say that the members of the so-called kinder platoon were HVOs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wore the same uniform. They were in Prozor. There was no other formation except the HVO there. How else can I explain it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And during that specific night, that night when they came at 2.00, did you see any insignia on their uniform? Did you see an insignia with HVO on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see them at all because I was in the basement. I learned from my wife, who had been there. I didn't see them myself. I didn't dare show myself. I was hiding in the dark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These members of the kinder platoon, you knew them or the other inhabitants of your village knew them. During the day were these people members of HVO units? At night we know that -- what they were doing, but what happened during the day? These people whom you name, Papak, et cetera, were they members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were very young, and I their parents, most of them. Later on, I would see them in the town, in the beginning, but who they belonged to I don't know. But the only unit was the HVO, so who else could they belong to but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How old was Papak, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were all between 16 and 20 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was Papak closer to 16 than to -- or to 20?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a little older. Some were very young. Pavkovic was very young. I know his father, and I knew him before the conflict. Vukoja was also young. I knew his father as well, Beljo. I knew some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A young Croat in Prozor, 20-year-old. Was such a person automatically mobilised into the ranks of the HVO, or was it possible for someone like that remain a civilian? Can you answer that question or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think he was a civilian, because he wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. We have concluded that I have spent enough time, so I will leave time for my colleagues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following counsel, please. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The counsel of Valentin Coric has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have any questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have maybe 10 minutes or even less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed. We have plenty of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon Mr. Islamovic. My name is Suzana Tomanovic. I'm an attorney from Bosnia and Herzegovina, counsel for Dr. Jadranko Prlic. Could we have put on e-court document P 00382. And while we are waiting for the document to show up on the screen, today you said during your testimony something which prompts me to put a question to you. When my colleague Ms. Alaburic showed you this decision on the appointment of the municipal Prozor HVO, you said you recognised all the names and that these men were men in high positions in government. First of all, let me tell you, is it true that Mr. Mijo Jozic, who was appointed president of the HVO in this decision, participated in the first parliamentary elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and was he elected president of Prozor municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a teacher of German, and at the first multi-party elections he was legally elected president of Prozor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: So we may conclude that as of the 13th of June, 1992, and Mr. Mate Boban issued the decision on his appointment, as president of the HVO for Prozor municipality, he in fact continued performing a duty for which -- or an office for which he had been democratically elected.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me with reference to the other names on this list, do you know what positions they held before the outbreak of the conflict? Nikola Ivic.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: He was a teacher of mechanics in school, and he was the committee secretary for a long time in the party.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The Communist Party, maybe four years or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: And after the election did he have any post?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Since he was the president of the HVO he was probably in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was referring to the elections of 1990.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about Mr. Ilija Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was the president of the HDZ. I am acquainted with him personally. I met him in the hospital in Rumbovci. He was the president of the HDZ. Whether he was the first president -- well, maybe he was even the first, I don't know, but I do know he was in the HDZ. I'm certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mile Tomic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mile Tomic had been a politician for many years. He was the director of the UNIS factory for a long time. And just before the war, I don't know what he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know what office he was elected to at the first multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stipo Curic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: He worked in the Territorial Defence before the war, and here I see that he was in the defence again.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marko Dragic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: He was a teacher of literature. For many years he was involved in politics in the socialist league. I think he was the president of the socialist league, Social Alliance or perhaps of the trade union.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilija Franic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: He was an HVO commander before Anto Pavlovic. I know that in the summer of 1993 he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what office he held after the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Until he was appointed to the staff, I don't know what he did. His sister had a house right next to mine. He often came to visit his sister. I knew his father. I don't think he held any office before he was appointed to the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the last on the list, Mr. Marko Loncar?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: He lived in the same building as I did. For 10 or 15 years he was in the municipal authorities. He was the municipal secretary. What else? I don't know any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know what office he held after the first multi-party elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know that. I know them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are talking about the elections. Witness, you are talking about the elections that took place in 1990. At the time of the elections of 1990, were Muslims elected to posts within the municipality? Because you, contrary to what you were saying earlier on, you seem to be very familiar with everything, and you seem to know everyone and to know what political side everyone was on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there weren't many parties, and it's a small place. Everybody knew everybody more or less. Of course, in 1990 there were Bosniaks in the police, because 35 per cent of the population in the municipality were Bosniaks. So of course they were in the authorities as well, but I don't recall right now who held what post or who was in government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because if we look at the list that we have in front of you, and you know that list because you know all these people, is there a Bosniak amongst them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm talking about 1993 -- no, 1992. I'm talking about the list we have in front of us, the list dated 12th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the HVO authorities. You can see for yourselves there are no Bosniaks among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for what reason according to you? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a power held by a single nation. They held all the power. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of at least one Muslim who held an office after the multi-party elections in the municipal authorities in 1990?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Hujdur was in the municipality. Hujdur. I can't remember his first name. Omer. Omer.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's no problem if you can't recall. Just a correction in the transcript. If it's still on the screen, I think that the gentleman said that 35 per cent of the politicians, not the policemen.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was referring to the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: So 35 per cent of the population?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was all. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Stojic has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, your Defence counsel does not wish to ask a question, but you do. What question is it that you wish to ask? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]. Some technical matters. I know the doctor well. I saw him fairly frequently. I was up there fairly often. So perhaps it will be best for us to try and clarify matters to see how they stood.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I am Slobodan Praljak. You are the doctor. We know each other. I'd just like to go through some basics first. I think the main problem we have to clarify is in my view the concept of what was there, the idea of what was going on there. It was very difficult to understand for anyone who wasn't there. It's difficult to understand what was going on up there, so let's try to explain the situation to all the counsel and to Their Honours as well what the situation was like up there. Now, do you remember that the houses of certain Croats were blown up by the Croats themselves, like the house belonging Bakitaric [as interpreted]? Do you remember that those people there --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bakitaric. Drugula Bakitaric, his house, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that those people there whose houses were blown up, that then Jozic the president of the municipality would usually -- that he -- they would come to president of the municipality usually with a pistol and ask for money? Do you know anything about that? Yes, no, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that Markesic's house, as you yourself know, that was one of them. And he was something in Sarajevo, in the HDZ or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: They blew his house to smithereens.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think he agreed politically. They didn't see eye to eye in politics.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And Did you know that the president of the municipality, Jozic, at one point in time when he couldn't take it any more, these people coming to him with a pistol got into his car, went to Germany, and never came back to Rama, Prozor, except for a church festival?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I know that his wife left, too, with the children. They left earlier on and I think he left in 1993 as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise for overlapping. Well, yes, at one point he left, too, because he couldn't take it any more. He got into his car and drove off. Now, do you know that a person called Misura from Rama, in the command in Rama, shot a whole burst of gunfire into a young guy from Tomislavgrad, and he was a paraplegic as a result? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that. I was in the health centre that night when it happened. It happened sometime around 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: He was a Croat? A Croat shooting at a Croat.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know of that incident.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that these bandits that went around at night at one time destroyed a whole transformer station and there was no electricity for a month and a half?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: In Rumboci yes I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, in Rama and Rumboci. Yes, I do apologise. I do apologise. We have enough time. I'm going to slow down. Do you know and I'm going to place a document on the ELMO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: At this speed the substance not coming through clearly any more. You have asked about the transformer station. The witness has said -- has named one locality. Then you answered by mentioning two localities. The witness did not confirm the second locality. So it's not just a matter of the comfort of the interpreters but also the Bench. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Quite correct. It's a question of logics. Thank you, Your Honour. And it's not always my logics that are at -- to blame but that clock over there. So I keep wanting to speed up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it happened in Rumboci. Slobodan Praljak thought it was in Rama. Well, it is in fact in Rama. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same thing. Now, Doctor, do you know how many times the HVO hospital in Rumboci was attacked by those gangs at night? Do you know whether it was attacked in the first place, and then --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I do know that it was attacked, yes, because I was there once, and on one night it was ridden with bullets -- riddled with bullets.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: May I now have P 01475 put on the ELMO -- on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but the -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] P 01475. P 01475. That's what it says here. That's the number. Here it is. The English version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You can read through this or have a look at it, Doctor. When Dr. Jozo Ivancevic came he informed you that on the 10th of February, 1993, at 0400 hours an armed attack was carried out against the military hospital by armed HVO members from the Rama area. And on that occasion, three Zolja type projectiles were launched. And later on in the document we can see what happened after that. The hand-held rocket launcher. And it says that Rama took in 3.560 wounded persons. Nobody complained of their work, but the same hospital was -- had already been attacked four times. You were able to read that just like me; right.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that in Rama 10 commanders of the Rama Brigade were replaced? And I'm just going to read out for 1993 which they were, Mr. Franic, up until the middle of January, 1993, then we have Zutic, then Beljo who died, who was killed, then we have Zelenika and Pavlovic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Andjelic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, Andjelic and others too. We won't go into that now. Now, do you know that in 1994, for instance, and you had left at that time, but anyway there was a conflict in Rama between the kinder platoon and the Garavi or blacks, with a lot of injured and wounded? Right. We'll go into that next time, on another occasion. Now, do you know that after the conflict that took place in Rama in 1992, in October, I arrived after those conflicts, I arrived up there, and that I stayed in the area until the end of 1992, Christmas of 1992? Do you know that nonetheless we succeeded with all the efforts that we invested to calm the situation down and to keep it under control in that turmoil of war right up until the all-out conflicts between the two armies of Bosnia and Herzegovina? As a doctor, were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, partially.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right, partially. I'd just like to ask you this now: Would you tell me -- or, rather, here in your statement -- I'm not quite sure, but I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You have made a rather long statement where you have given a lot of information, and then the witness says, "Yes, I partially agree." This is of zero worth for the Bench, because we do not to what he actually agrees. There's a whole parcel of information. I think it would be preferable if you could cut it down. One question, one answer. Because otherwise we are lost. I'm sorry. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're quite right. I cannot, in view of the fact that this witness was not in politics or anything else, I can only ask him some limited information, whether after 1992 for a long time we were able to maintain some sort of law and order, all of us together. When I say "us," I mean all of us together although I wasn't there for quite some time. So that's all I wanted to ask and establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak asked you the question, Witness, and he said that he arrived in the area and that according to him, and that's his analysis of the situation, the situation calmed down, because before he arrived, as he said, there were problems there. Now, did you notice that? Did you notice tangible change once General Praljak had arrived? Your answer was yes. You said "yes, partially," but could you tell us what that yes referred to and explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know what General Praljak arrived exactly but after the first conflicts in Prozor in 1992, October, or rather the 23rd of October 1992, up until, let's say, May when the conflicts in Jablanica, Konjic and Mostar broke out, not many things -- many not terrible things happened if you compare this to the situation later on when the conflict broke out in Jablanica, Konjic, Mostar, and so on and so forth. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. There's a problem that we have to clear up here. When in France, for example, or in America we meet a soldier wearing a uniform and we see that he has done something, then with a great degree of certainty we can assume that he's a French soldier or an American soldier. Now, here the problem is this: With the HVO and -- or BH army, we have the following problem, and do you share my opinion? I'd like to ask you that, that everybody could buy a uniform and wear a uniform and that everybody wore a uniform, both people in --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... defendant keeps making these statements all the time and not putting questions to this witness. Are we to assume that Mr. Praljak is now giving evidence not under oath? I'm just at a loss as far as where this is going.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, madam. Just a moment. My question was very clear. Does the doctor --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I hadn't actually heard a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please proceed, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Does the doctor share my opinion, does the doctor agree when I say that an HVO uniform of the uniform of the BH army was a uniform that anybody could buy and wear at any time regardless of whether he was in a unit or not, whether it was an HVO unit or BH army unit? So does the doctor share my opinion? He can say no, but my question is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: All men, and women, too, who were active wore uniforms, camouflage uniforms with HVO insignia, as far as I know.
