utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And did people wear uniforms who were just able to buy uniforms with this HVO insignia who had nothing to do with the army at all?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they didn't have to even buy uniforms because there were so many uniforms readily available. They could just put on a uniform. Anybody could.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear. That's my first question and the answer to it. Now, my second question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Dr. Islamovic, you said that everybody had walked around in an HVO uniform; right? Did you, for instance, walk around in an HVO uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So it was not everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had my white doctor's coat, and I was in the health centre, and when I went home I was wearing civilian clothes in 1993, when I was off duty. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Doctor, you know the area well. Now, how many villages and hamlets are there in the Prozor municipality? Roughly speaking, 50, 60, 70, how many?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: About 50.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, during the day was the situation tolerable and intolerable during the night? That's my question. During the day was there some sort of law and order? And then night came, night fell, and 50 villages and hamlets were raided by gangs who were out of control. So I'm just trying to check what kind of power and authority anybody had, responsibility, individuals, groups of individuals, what kind of power could they have, could they control 50 or 60 villages and hamlets when night-time came and these gangs turned up, with the best will in the world were they able to do anything?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult to control the situation, yes. Usually they would get to the nearer villages, but the far-off villages, I'm thinking about the Bosniak inhabitants, after April, 1993, for instance, one by one towards Jablanica, the border towards Jablanica, the area was set on fire. The army, the soldiers, would turn up and expel the population and force them closer and closer into town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, I have a question, a follow-up question. You yourself, when you were in Prozor, did you have a vehicle of some sort, a car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the cars were confiscated from the Muslims after the conflict in 1992, in October. After that, if somebody managed to hide something somewhere but no had a car. Nobody had a telephone. They had switched off all the telephones. And I didn't have a car either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, did you ever leave Prozor to have to go to some of the neighbouring villages, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to know whether in case you had to leave town whether you went through any checkpoints, but you tell me that you didn't leave town. Continue, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, still a question in relation to this. If you never left Prozor, how can you as a witness under oath talk about 50, 60 hamlets in the whole area of Prozor? If you have not been there, how -- how come you know? Are you an expert in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that I had been a physician for 15 years in that particular municipality, so I knew all those villages and hamlets and visited them thousands of times more or less. And there's not a single village or hamlet or house where I had not been at some time for vaccines, for home visits, things like that. I went to all the schools, visited all the schools, so I know the whole area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am not -- I am not doubting that at all, but the questions relate to what happened in -- mainly in 1993. That's what your testimony is about. And at that time you had no possibility to go there. So how do you know what happened at that time in those hamlets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you hear about things. You hear about everything. If there's a problem somewhere, people hear about it. Somebody from the village comes into town. A villager turns up. You hear about someone being expelled and that the village or hamlet had been torched, things like that. But no, I didn't go. Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just a few more questions, Doctor. You will remember that apart from the Territorial Defence and the HVO in 1992 there was the HOS. HOS was in the area with its military organisation, with its army, with its weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more thing. When you were expelled from your job, that was when Bugojno fell or liberation of Bugojno, depending on which side you're on, how you look at things, anyway in that place, Bugojno, according to our records there are about 3.700 HVO soldiers and many more thousand civilians from there and the surrounding villages, and they all came in, whether by car or on foot. And apart from that is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And the offensive launched by the BH army continued towards Vakuf with the clear military desire to control and take over Vakuf, Uskoplje?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Gillett. I don't understand your objection because the witness of his own accord did say that following on from the Bugojno events he was up on the hill and he saw columns of cars and buses arriving. Now, the question is quite logical, and I myself was going to ask it. Go ahead. Sit down, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, in the population census of 1992 in Prozor, Rama, there were 12.300 Croats, Croat inhabitants, roughly, and then as many came in from Bugojno, plus the people that were there beforehand. Would that be correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: [Interpretation] He said yes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpratation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So we now see something that I wish to establish with your help. In an area that was destroyed such as Rama, with tense inter-ethnic relations, you had as many Croat inhabitants coming in as lived in that place under normal conditions. Was that the situation? Was that the picture? Was that the kind of situation that we had to deal with?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as soon as you had so many people coming in there was a problem, the problem of accommodation, the problem of soldiers and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And what you said, Doctor, when the women came to ask for buses to leave the area, do you share my opinion that the most terrible thing for responsible individuals was at that time that feeling of impotence, their impotence to prevent what they felt was going to happen and did not allow -- could not let people go into other areas where they thought there would be ethnic cleansing? I think that's the number one dilemma that was posed during that war.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Because Jozic, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, just a moment. General Praljak has just said that there were thousands of Croats coming in from Bugojno, and you yourself, on the basis of what I was able to understand, were a spectator. You observed those people. Now, among all those people arriving, pouring in, were there any HVO soldiers amongst the people? Not from Prozor but who were coming in from Bugojno. Did you see them arrive? Did you see HVO soldiers coming in?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: That morning when I set out from my flat in my car, it was a Renault 4, I saw -- there's just one street. I saw lots of uniformed soldiers mixed with civilians coming in from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, your Renault 4 car, it hadn't been confiscated yet then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not my car. I said that it was actually my neighbour's car. He was from down by Jablanica way, so he transported us for 20 marks a distance of 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And you said that you saw uniformed soldiers; is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And those uniformed soldiers coming from Bugojno on the basis of what you were aware of or came to know about, did they stay in the area or did they go on elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that. I don't know how many of them stayed in Prozor. I think some of them stayed in Prozor and others went to Croatia perhaps and so on. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Doctor, my last question -- or, rather, I'd just like to check something out. In your statement you say that two prisoners turned up. One was Perviz, hit in his abdominal area with a bullet and the other was Dervis hit in the back and the bullet remained in his body. Am I right in thinking that they did manage to transport them to the hospital in Split?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think you're wrong on that score because this man Perviz, who was shot in the stomach, well, he would have of died had he actually been hit in the stomach. But it was an entry/exit wound. It went through one part of his tissue and exited. Whereas the other man was probably shot from a distance and the bullet was lodged just underneath his skin here. So they weren't seriously wounded. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I just wanted to check that out, because I seem to remember that we used a helicopter to transport some wounded Muslims, whether a woman or who I don't know.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, these men were not seriously injured.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you for everything. Thank you for coming, and thank you for telling us truthfully what happened. So I thank you in my own name. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well. All the Defence counsel have conducted their cross-examinations. Are there any additional questions from the Prosecution, because we still have several minutes left? Madam Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No, no questions from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Doctor, on behalf of the Judges before you, I should like to thank you to coming to The Hague to testify. I wish you a bon voyage back home and would like to say thank you for your testimony. I'm going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, with respect to the tendering of exhibits, I turn to the Prosecution first. Any documents to tender, Ms. Gillett? Prosecution exhibits which you would like to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that I already tendered them at the close of questions from the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What about the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one document. P 01475. It is a document presented to the witness about the shelling of the hospital by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one exhibit. Prosecution Exhibit P 00382. It is a decision by Mate Boban on the appointment of the municipal Prozor HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber accords -- admits these documents into evidence, the witness statement, as well as the documents presented to the witness, which were referenced under the following numbers: 344 -- 3091, 3286, 4193, 8994, 8998, 9685, 9686, 9687, and also the Defence exhibits, documents P 01475 for Mr. Kovacic and Exhibit P 00382 for Counsel Alaburic. That's the documents taken care of. Now, for tomorrow, Mr. Mundis, what is the programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, tomorrow we will commence with the witness Mulahusic whose testimony will be led by Rule 89(F). My understanding from speaking to one of my colleagues is the next witness on the schedule will also be a Rule 89(F) witness, which is a change in the plans in order to expedite the proceedings for this week followed by the final witness scheduled who we previously announced would be a Rule 89(F) witness as well with the consequence, Your Honours, that the remaining witnesses for this week will all be led by way of Rule 89(F) so as to maximise the likelihood that we will finish hearing these three witnesses during the two days that are left for us this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Everything is crystal clear now. As you know, we will reconvene tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00. I hope that Mr. Pusic will get well in the meantime, and I'll see you tomorrow. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th day of September, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: [The accused Pusic not present in court]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.,
